sections.text: 3 Characterizing Reasoning Trace Quality In this section, we introduce ME 2 principle , a concise principle for characterizing reasoning trace quality that goes beyond linear, step-wise level and accounts for both local step validity and global structural organization. 3.1 Overview Modeling reasoning quality requires considerations along multiple axes. In terms of granularity, global structural organization governs how branches are introduced, explored, and resolved ( macro-level ), while fine-grained step content determines the validity of local inferences ( micro-level ). In terms of objectives, traces often exhibit redundancy that increases inference cost and exacerbate long-context issues ( efficiency ) ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . At the same time, a trace should make genuine progress toward a well-justified conclusion, maintaining logical coherence and staying aligned with the problem ( effectiveness ) ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Barez et al., 2025 ) . Motivated by these considerations, we introduce ME 2 principle as a unified characterization of reasoning trace quality that disentangles where quality manifests (macro vs. micro) and what quality entails (efficiency vs. effectiveness), as illustrated in Fig. 2 . Figure 2 : The ME 2 principle , characterizing reasoning trace quality along macro/micro granularity and efficiency/effectiveness. 3.2 ME 2 principle Macro-Efficiency. Whether the reasoning structure is well organized, avoiding unnecessary branching and reflection. A macro-efficient trace maintains a controlled reasoning structure, introduces or closes branches only when needed, and applies reflection or verification selectively to guide subsequent steps. Macro-efficiency degrades when traces repeatedly reopen completed branches or perform redundant restarts and rechecks that fail to advance the main line of reasoning ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Macro-Effectiveness. Whether the reasoning structure remains logically coherent and aligned with the problem objective. A macro-effective trace remains on target with respect to the problem and exhibits a smooth, well-articulated line of reasoning across structurally adjacent steps. In contrast, macro-effectiveness degrades when branch objectives are underspecified, topics shift abruptly, or the trace makes illogical shortcuts ( Barez et al., 2025 ) . Such failures are especially common in hard problems, where superficially plausible yet invalid arguments may emerge (e.g., pseudo-proofs in challenging mathematical tasks) ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) . Micro-Efficiency. Whether individual steps avoid local redundancy. A micro-efficient trace consists of concise, purposeful steps that perform concrete operations, such as explicit calculations or decisive validity checks, expressed in clear and direct terms. In contrast, micro-efficiency degrades when steps contain redundant statements or wording, unnecessary hedging or modifiers, or looping patterns that repeat prior content without refinement ( Li et al., 2025a ) . Micro-Effectiveness. Whether individual steps are locally valid and internally consistent. A micro-effective trace consists of steps that provide explicit justifications, perform coherent and well-founded computations, and use consistent notation and assumptions. In contrast, micro-effectiveness degrades when steps contain local errors, e.g., contradictions, hallucinations, unsupported claims, or incorrect arithmetic ( Lightman et al., 2023 ; Lee and Hockenmaier, 2025 ) .

4 Evaluating Reasoning Traces In this section, based on the ME 2 principle , we propose an automated evaluation framework that supports reliable pairwise comparison and underpins the reward model training. Figure 3 : Macro- and micro-level abstractions over a reasoning DAG with three canonical structures (progression, branching, and merging). Edges are directed from top to bottom, and node indices indicate step order. Progression : linear continuation. Branching : a node expands into multiple child nodes. Merging : multiple parent nodes converge into a single child node. 4.1 Step Partitioning Given a raw reasoning trace s s , we partition it into atomic reasoning steps. We start with a coarse segmentation by splitting s s on “ \n\n ”, producing multiple base blocks. To obtain more stable step boundaries across heterogeneous traces, we refine this partition using step-prefix patterns. Specifically, we extract the leading tokens (e.g., the first word) of each base block and compute their frequencies over a large corpus of traces. High-frequency prefixes are then used as refined delimiters to re-partition s s into steps ( s 1 , … , s n ) (s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) . This procedure yields consistent and semantically meaningful step boundaries across models ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) (See App. D for details and prefix statistics). 4.2 Reasoning Structuring As noted in Sec. 2 , directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) offer a natural abstraction for reasoning traces. Given partitioned steps ( s 1 , … , s n ) (s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) , we model the underlying reasoning structure as a DAG G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) , where each node v i ∈ V v_{i}\in V corresponds to the step s i s_{i} , and each directed edge e ∈ E e\in E encodes a semantic dependency between steps. The central goal is to construct the edge set E E , thereby transforming unstructured steps into a structured DAG. Such representation naturally expresses three canonical reasoning patterns: progression, branching, and merging, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . Since reasoning steps are generated sequentially, the observed order ( v 1 , … , v n ) (v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}) can be viewed as a topological ordering of G G ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . We therefore construct G G incrementally by traversing the steps in order and, for each node v i v_{i} , selecting its parent nodes from earlier steps to form directed edges leading into v i v_{i} . Concretely, we define an attachment pool 𝒫 i ⊆ { v 1 , … , v i − 1 } \mathcal{P}_{i}\subseteq\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}\} as the candidate parent set for v i v_{i} , and prompt an LLM to select Parent ⁡ ( v i ) ⊆ 𝒫 i \mathrm{Parent}(v_{i})\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{i} based on semantic continuity and transition cues. To avoid exposing the LLM to excessively long contexts, 𝒫 i \mathcal{P}_{i} includes a subset of nodes rather than the full set { v 1 , … , v i − 1 } \{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}\} , consisting of (i) the nodes along the current main branch from the root to v i − 1 v_{i-1} and (ii) a small set of representative branch endpoints (see App. E for construction details and App. J.1 for the prompt design). This design is sufficient in practice for recovering accurate parent relations. Finally, to obtain a compact structure, we compress the DAG by collapsing consecutive linear chains of nodes into super-nodes , each representing a semantically continuous reasoning span (e.g., nodes 2 and 4 in Fig. 3 can form a super-node). The node set V V is replaced by these super-nodes, while the structure presented by edge set E E remains unchanged. This procedure is summarized in Alg. 1 , with representative DAG examples shown in App. K.1 Fig. 18 . To make the comparison robust and tractable, we transform each trace into complementary abstractions that separately capture macro-level structure and micro-level step quality. Macro-level Abstraction. For the DAG G G , we construct a concise structural narrative reflecting its global organization. Let V = { v 1 , … , v t } V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{t}\} denote the set of super-nodes. For each v k ∈ V v_{k}\in V , we prompt an LLM to generate a short summary a k a_{k} describing its intent, key intermediate conclusions, and structural role. These summaries are then linearized into a compact textual sequence 𝒜 macro ​ ( G ) = ( a 1 , … , a t ) \mathcal{A}_{\text{macro}}(G)=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}) using a simple traversal scheme with explicit structural annotations (details in App. J.2 ). This abstraction makes the global structure of the reasoning explicit, enabling macro-level assessment without being distracted by low-level verbosity. Micro-level Abstraction. To evaluate local reasoning quality, we focus on the dominant path π ⁡ ( G ) \pi(G) , defined as the main trajectory from the root node to the node corresponding to the final answer (details in App. J.3 ). Although auxiliary branches may explore alternatives or verification steps, π ⁡ ( G ) \pi(G) concentrates the sequence of steps that most directly support the final conclusion. We therefore use 𝒜 micro ​ ( G ) = π ​ ( G ) \mathcal{A}_{\text{micro}}(G)=\pi(G) as the primary evidence for micro-level evaluation. Hierarchical Evaluation. Given two traces, following ME 2 principle , we compare them at the macro abstraction 𝒜 macro ​ ( G ) \mathcal{A}_{\text{macro}}(G) and the micro abstraction 𝒜 micro ​ ( G ) \mathcal{A}_{\text{micro}}(G) , evaluating efficiency and effectiveness at each level and producing four dimension-wise judgments { ( y d , r d ) } d = 1 4 \{(y_{d},r_{d})\}_{d=1}^{4} , where y d ∈ { a ≻ b , b ≻ a , tie } y_{d}\in\{a\succ b,b\succ a,\text{tie}\} and r d r_{d} is a brief natural-language rationale. Each judgment is produced by an LLM using its corresponding dimension-specific prompt (App. J.4 ), and the resulting judgments and rationales are aggregated by the LLM into an overall preference ( y , r ) (y,r) for downstream reward modeling, where y ∈ { a ≻ b , b ≻ a , tie } y\in\{a\succ b,b\succ a,\text{tie}\} . Since pairwise judgments can be sensitive to presentation order (i.e., position bias ( Shi et al., 2024 ) ), we evaluate each pair under both original and reversed orderings to enable robust evaluation , repeating the comparison multiple times and retaining only consistent, non-tied labels.

5 Optimizing Reasoning with Thinking Rewards In this section, we show how the proposed ME 2 principle and the resulting Thinking Reward Model (TRM) can be used to optimize reasoning in practice. We first describe how we construct pairwise preference data and train TRM, and then demonstrate how TRM supports both test-time scaling and reinforcement learning, enabling models to internalize higher-quality reasoning behaviors. 5.1 Reward Modeling Dataset Construction. We construct the TRM-Preference dataset from WebInstruct-verified ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , which contains verifiable STEM and math problems requiring non-trivial multi-step reasoning. We sample 64K prompts and generate candidate reasoning traces 1 1 1 A reasoning trace refers to the generated reasoning content before the reasoning-termination marker (e.g., </think> ). using multiple open-source reasoning model families, including Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , DeepSeek-Distill ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , and GPT-OSS ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . To decouple reasoning quality from answer correctness, we retain only traces whose final answers are verified as correct , as correctness can be reliably assessed by rule-based verifiers, allowing the learned reward signal to focus on reasoning quality rather than duplicating answer-based supervision. For each prompt, we generate multiple candidate reasoning traces and apply the evaluation pipeline described in Sec. 4 to construct reasoning structures and perform pairwise preference judgments under the ME 2 principle , using DeepSeek-V3.2 ( Liu et al., 2025 ) as an automated evaluator. To avoid over-representation of individual prompts, we sample at most four trace pairs per prompt. This process yields 103K training pairs and a held-out validation set of 1.5K pairs, forming the final TRM-Preference dataset. Additional details are provided in App. F , with illustrative case studies of the constructed DAGs shown in App. K.1 Fig. 18 . TRM Training. We initialize TRM from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) by replacing the language modeling head with a scalar value head, and train it on the TRM-Preference dataset using the Bradley–Terry loss ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ) , following standard preference modeling practice ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Kirk et al., 2023 ) . Training details and dynamics are provided in App. G.1 , and the Bradley–Terry formulation is summarized in App. I . 5.2 Validation Set Analysis Table 1 : Pairwise preference evaluation on the validation set. √ \surd , ∼ \sim , and × \times denote correct, tied, and incorrect judgments, respectively. The top and bottom rows correspond to using Qwen3-8B and GPT-OSS-20B as the response models, respectively. Evaluation Protocol and Results. We evaluate TRM on the validation set against three baselines: ReasonFlux-PRM-7B ( Zou et al., 2025 ) , Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , and PromptOnly . PromptOnly applies our pairwise evaluation prompts (App. J.4 ) with DeepSeek-V3.2 ( Liu et al., 2025 ) to raw, unstructured traces, using the same robust protocol in Sec. 4.3 to reduce position bias. As shown in Tab. 1 , TRM achieves the highest accuracy, as expected. ReasonFlux-PRM-7B captures part of the preference signal (62.5%), likely due to its focus on local step-level effectiveness (see App. C.1 for further discussion), while Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B performs close to random, consistent with its limited modeling of long-range and structural reasoning observed in Zou et al. (2025) . Limitations of Direct Prompt-Based Evaluation. The prompt-based DeepSeek-V3.2 evaluator ranks second but produces a large number of ties (232); when ties are excluded, its accuracy reaches 93%, indicating that our constructed preference data is reliable and that non-tied pairs typically exhibit clear quality differences. However, the high tie rate exposes a fundamental limitation of direct prompt-based evaluation: many reasoning trace pairs differ primarily in how reasoning steps are organized and consolidated, rather than in local step content. Such differences (e.g., redundant branching or illogical shortcuts, as characterized by ME 2 principle ) are weakly expressed in flat, unstructured traces and are therefore difficult to distinguish via direct prompt-based comparison. By explicitly modeling reasoning structure, our DAG-based abstractions (Sec. 4 ) surface these signals and enable more fine-grained and discriminative assessment aligned with the ME 2 principle . 5.3 TRM-Guided Test-Time Scaling Table 2 : Main results across multiple benchmarks. We evaluate TRM in test-time scaling ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) with Best-of- N N selection, where rewards are used to select the highest-scoring output from generated traces. Under this setup, TRM favors traces that best aligns with the ME 2 principle . We compare TRM against representative PRMs, including ReasonFlux-PRM-7B ( Zou et al., 2025 ) and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , using GPT-OSS-20B ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) and Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as response models. Experiments are conducted on AIME24 and AIME25, with each setting repeated five times for robustness. Additional experimental details are provided in App. G.2 . From Better Reasoning to Better Outcomes. Although TRM models only reasoning trace quality without considering user-facing responses, and is trained exclusively on verified-correct traces without any explicit correctness supervision, we still observe a clear correspondence between better reasoning and better final outcomes. As shown in Fig. 4 , selecting traces that are more aligned with the ME 2 principle consistently improves Best-of- N N accuracy as N N increases. In contrast, existing PRMs such as ReasonFlux-PRM-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM explicitly incorporate correctness-oriented supervision during training ( Zou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Despite this difference, TRM achieves comparable or even superior performance, with gains of up to 19.3% (e.g., from 44.7% at N = 1 N=1 to 64.0% at N = 16 N=16 on AIME24 with Qwen3-8B), demonstrating that better reasoning, as measured by closer alignment with the ME 2 principle, leads to better final outcomes . 5.4 TRM-Guided RL Optimization Thinking Reward Signals. To explore how TRM improves reasoning quality during training, we adopt reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2025 ) and integrate TRM as an auxiliary reward signal within Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . GRPO optimizes a binary verifiable reward r v ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{v}\in\{0,1\} that enforces outcome correctness, treating all reasoning traces that yield the same answer as equivalent. In contrast, TRM provides a thinking reward r t r_{t} that evaluates the quality of the underlying reasoning trace. Since it is trained exclusively on verified-correct traces, r t r_{t} is used to rank and shape alternative correct reasoning paths. Consider the RLVR objective with a binary verifiable reward r v ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{v}\in\{0,1\} and the gated reward r r defined in Eq. 1 . This clarifies the role of TRM in providing richer optimization signals that bias learning toward ME 2 principle among correct traces. Settings. Based on the WebInstruct-Verified dataset ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , we train three models with varying reasoning capabilities: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . As baselines, we consider two reward signals: (1) Verifier , which relies solely on the verifiable reward r v r_{v} provided by a verifier, and (2) ReasonFlux-PRM-7B , a strong PRM that evaluates reasoning trace quality at the step level using the same reward formulation in Eq. 1 . The weighting parameter α \alpha is fixed to 0.2. Additional experimental details and training settings are provided in App. G.3 . Figure 5 : Pairwise win rates (ties excluded) across different policy models . TRM, Verifier, and ReasonFlux denote policies trained with our TRM, the verifiable reward r v r_{v} , and ReasonFlux-PRM-7B, respectively. Each bar reports the win rate of Model A against Model B. Benchmarks. We use 10 representative and challenging benchmarks covering diverse domains and difficulty levels. For general reasoning, we use GPQA-Diamond ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , SuperGPQA ( Du et al., 2025 ) , MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , BBEH ( Kazemi et al., 2025 ) , and FrontierScience (FS) ( OpenAI, 2025 ) . For mathematical reasoning, we use AMC, AIME24, AIME25, MATH500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , and Olympiad ( He et al., 2024 ) , using AVG@32 on AIME24 and AIME25 for robustness. From Thinking Rewards to Training Gains. As reported in Tab. 2 , TRM outperforms both the Verifier and ReasonFlux-PRM-7B. Compared to the Verifier baseline, TRM improves performance by approximately 2%–4%, with the largest gains on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (3.9% on STEM and 3.8% on Math). TRM also surpasses ReasonFlux-PRM-7B, with particularly strong improvements on challenging benchmarks such as GPQA, AIME24, and AIME25, indicating that thinking rewards provide an effective training signal beyond verifiable reward. The ablation study in App. H further supports the choice of α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 .

6 Analysis 6.1 TRM Improves Reasoning Quality In this section, we provide empirical comparisons and case studies to investigate how TRM improves reasoning quality. Figure 6 : Training dynamics of Qwen2.5-Math-7B: (a) TRM scores and (b) test accuracy under verifier-guided and TRM-guided RL optimization. Test accuracy is evaluated on tasks with rule-based verifiers (i.e., excluding FrontierScience ( OpenAI, 2025 ) ). Empirical Comparison. We evaluate reasoning quality by applying the checkpoints trained in Sec. 5.4 to AIME24, AIME25, and GPQA-Diamond, and conduct pairwise evaluation following Sec. 4 with DeepSeek-V3.2 as the evaluator across the four dimensions of ME 2 principle . As shown in Fig. 5 , TRM-trained policies consistently outperform the BaseModel, Verifier-trained, and ReasonFlux-trained policies in reasoning quality. These improvements indicate that distilling ME 2 principle into TRM and using it as a supervision signal during training effectively enhances the quality of reasoning produced by the policy model. Case Study. We further provide qualitative case studies to explore how thinking rewards relate to reasoning quality in practice. In App. K.2 and App. K.3 , we compare reasoning traces generated under identical prompts by a TRM-trained policy and a baseline, and observe that the TRM-trained policy follows a more disciplined reasoning trajectory that is more closely aligned with ME 2 principle . In App. K.4 and App. K.5 , we analyze two reasoning traces scored by our TRM and find that the higher-scoring trace exhibits clearer structure and greater efficiency under the proposed ME 2 principle . In Fig. 6 (a), TRM-guided RL yields a steadily increasing thinking reward throughout training. In contrast, verifier-guided RL, despite showing an early improvement in reasoning quality, quickly plateaus, with reasoning behaviors converging in the mid-to-late stages.
